expectations_used.clarify: Reads the failing test body and asks whether partially shipped holds should return only unshipped units before editing.
expectations_used.approach: Names the mechanism — the sweep releasing the original count rather than the remaining count — not merely "something in the sweep".
expectations_used.communicate: Narrates what the failure diff shows and which hold-state fields are being traced.
expectations_used.implement: Changes the sweep's released-quantity computation to test the stated hypothesis.
expectations_used.verify: Re-runs the suite and confirms the partially-shipped expiry test passes without breaking full-release behavior.
expectations_used.reflect: Explains why releasing the original count created phantom stock and how the remaining-count fix prevents it.

summary: The candidate fixated on holds/createHold.ts for the entire session based on an early hunch, making several unfocused edits there without ever inspecting or touching sweep.ts, where the actual bug (releasing original count instead of remaining count) lived. They briefly voiced the exact right question about partial shipments reducing released units but abandoned it immediately, and ended the session without re-running tests or reaching the real root cause.

dimensions.analysis: The candidate did raise the exact right question at +440s about whether partial shipments should reduce released units — this is precisely the crux of the actual bug. But instead of pausing to investigate or seeking confirmation, they immediately dismissed their own good instinct and kept assuming the bug was in hold creation, never revisiting it.

The candidate never named a specific mechanism; they anchored early on createHold.ts based on a vague feeling of familiarity and stayed there for the whole session despite no test evidence pointing to that file. Even their one strong hypothesis about partial shipments and released units was voiced but abandoned without exploration, leaving them working off a location guess (creation logic) rather than a mechanism.

The candidate narrated a fairly continuous stream of thoughts throughout — what they suspected, what they were about to edit, and their confidence level — so an interviewer could follow their (misguided) path even though the narration revealed uncertainty and drift rather than sharp reasoning.

All edits were confined to holds/createHold.ts across many iterations — deadline calc, expiry setting, units validation — with no coherent throughline connecting them, and no edits ever touched sweep.ts where the actual bug lived. This is scattered probing rather than execution of a stated, falsifiable plan.
The candidate never re-ran the test suite after their initial failing run at +6s; they saved multiple times and declared fair confidence at the end without any check that the failing test now passed.

The session ends with a vague statement of being fairly confident, but no articulation of what the actual root cause was or why any specific edit fixed it — consistent with the fact that they never touched the actual buggy file (sweep.ts) and the test almost certainly still failed.
